title: Women in the Middle Ages
objective: After this level you can describe the lives, work and power of medieval women.
summary: By class and region: Christine de Pizan wrote for a living, Margaret Paston ran estates, brewsters and Paris silkwomen worked in trade, and coverture limited wives.

cards.headline: In 1405 a French widow built a city out of words.
cards.body: Its citizens were famous women, and its author, Christine de Pizan, is a good guide to what medieval women could do, and what they couldn’t.

cards.headline: Living by the pen
cards.body: Christine de Pizan (1364 to about 1430) was widowed after ten years of marriage, with three children to raise. She took up writing to support them. In The Book of the City of Ladies (1405) she wrote of women known for heroism and virtue, and she defended women against misogynist satire. She argued back, in print, and it paid the bills.

cards.headline: Running the estate
cards.body: In England, the gentry had their own formidable women. Margaret Paston (about 1421 to 1484) was a Norfolk gentlewoman. She left the largest collection of personal letters from medieval England, many to her husband while he was away. While he was away she managed the family’s estates, and when attackers threatened their manor house she defended it and asked him for crossbows and armour.

cards.headline: Women at work
cards.body: In towns and villages, women worked for money. Women brewed and sold most of the ale drunk in medieval England; after 1350, men slowly took over the trade. In 13th- and 14th-century Paris, the silk industry even had some all-female guilds, and a few silkwomen did business with aristocrats and the king himself.

cards.headline: The legal limits
cards.body: The law set hard limits too. Under English coverture, rooted in Norman custom, a wife’s legal existence was suspended: she could not make contracts or sue in her own name, though a single woman could. So what a medieval woman could do depended heavily on her class, her region and whether she was married.
cards.callout: Class, place and marriage shaped a medieval woman’s options

cards.headline: Women in the Middle Ages: understood
learned: Christine de Pizan wrote to support her family
Margaret Paston ran and defended her family’s estates
Women brewed most English ale; Paris had women’s silk guilds
Coverture limited married women in English law

questions.prompt: How did the widowed Christine de Pizan support herself and her three children?

options.label: By brewing and selling ale
options.rationale: That was the work of English brewsters.

options.label: By running a Paris silk guild

questions.explanation: Widowed after ten years of marriage, Christine took up writing to support herself and her three children.

questions.prompt: Under English coverture, why couldn’t a married woman usually make a contract in her own name?

options.label: Women were not allowed to learn to write
options.rationale: Many could; Margaret Paston ran affairs by letter.

options.label: Her legal existence was suspended during marriage
Only guild masters could sign contracts
options.rationale: Contracts were not limited to guilds.

options.label: The Church forbade all contracts by laypeople
options.rationale: Coverture was a rule of English law.

questions.explanation: Coverture suspended a wife’s legal existence, so she could not contract or sue in her own name; a single woman could.

questions.prompt: Level 53’s guilds ranked masters, journeymen and apprentices. What was unusual about some of medieval Paris’s silk guilds?

options.label: They had no apprentices at all
options.rationale: The unusual thing was who ran them.

options.label: They were run by the king
options.rationale: Some silkwomen sold to the king; they didn’t work for him.

options.label: They met only once a year

questions.explanation: Paris’s 13th- and 14th-century silk industry had some all-female guilds.
